title: A Randomized Study of a Strength Training Program to Prevent Injuries in Runners of the New York City Marathon
authors: Toresdahl BG, McElheny K, Metzl J, Ammerman B, Chang B, Kinderknecht J
population: First-time New York City Marathon runners aged 18 or older (mean age 35.9, 69.4% female); 720 enrolled, 583 started, 579 completed
findings: Randomized 12 weeks before the marathon to a self-directed 10-minute strength program done 3 times weekly (quadriceps, hip abductor, core; written and video instruction) or an observation group.
Overuse injury causing marathon noncompletion occurred in 7.1% (strength) versus 7.3% (observation); RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.57-1.63; P = 0.90).
Major injury incidence was 8.9% and minor injury 48.5%; 52 of 64 major injuries were overuse, of which 20 were bone stress injuries.
Finishing time was 5 h 1 min versus 4 h 58 min (P = 0.35).
limitations: Self-directed program with unmeasured adherence; self-reported injuries; novice first-time marathoners, mostly female; only 10 minutes of low-load work; noncompletion is a late, rare outcome so the trial is underpowered for minor injury.
implications: Do not claim that a short, self-directed bodyweight routine prevents running injuries.
For first-time marathoners prioritize gradual mileage progression and adherence; keep strength as a low-cost addition.
Flag bone stress injury risk in novice marathon plans by capping weekly load increases rather than relying on strength.

verification.notes: Corrected the researcher's '20 of 64 major injuries were bone stress injuries': the abstract states 52 of 64 major injuries were overuse, 20 of which were bone stress injuries. Crossref year 2019 (online-first), Europe PMC 2020.
